enrichment.short_title: Section 55 asylum support refusals and destitution
key_facts: Six consolidated judicial review claims challenged NASS refusals of asylum support under section 55 after claims were not made at port or immediately on arrival.
Section 55, in force from 8 January 2003, prohibits support unless the Secretary of State is satisfied the asylum claim was made as soon as reasonably practicable after arrival.
Refused claimants were left destitute, sleeping rough unless charities or individuals assisted them.
Sample claimants included port arrivals who said agents told them not to claim at immigration, lorry arrivals, and traumatised young asylum seekers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated judicial review of section 55 asylum support refusals, listed as lead cases to give early guidance.
enrichment.outcome: Claims succeeded; attacked refusals were to be quashed and reconsidered; interim support and fair decision-making guidance given.
enrichment.ratio: Section 55(1) requires an objective assessment of whether, in all the claimant's circumstances, the asylum claim was made as soon as reasonably practicable, so agent advice may be a valid reason; decision-making must be fair and adequately reasoned; and section 55(5) means that leaving an asylum seeker without support will normally breach Articles 3 and 8 where destitution creates a real risk to health, while the absence of a fact-finding appeal engages Article 6.
legal_issues: Construction of 'as soon as reasonably practicable' under section 55(1)
Fairness of NASS decision-making without interview or appeal
Whether section 55(5) prevents support refusals that would leave claimants destitute
Compatibility with Articles 3, 6 and 8 ECHR
Whether Article 14 is engaged
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for Social Security ex parte JCWI
Khawaja v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R (Alconbury) v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Core ratio, human rights holdings, and quashing outcome are explicit in the judgment and oral ruling. Judge metadata in the source file lists multiple historical names and may be unreliable.

enrichment.short_title: Joint authorship and revocation of implied copyright licence
key_facts: Session violinist Bobby Valentino claimed joint authorship of the Bluebells' 1984 recording of 'Young at Heart'.
The trial judge found he wrote the memorable violin introduction and was a 50% joint copyright owner.
From 1984 to 1993 Valentino impliedly licensed Hodgens to exploit the work without claiming royalties.
After the song's 1993 chart revival following use in a Volkswagen advert, Valentino claimed a share of future royalties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by Hodgens against liability findings and against rejection of proprietary estoppel defences; limited permission on section 11(3).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal on section 11(3) refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 11(3) does not require a common intention to create joint authorship beyond collaboration producing a non-separate contribution; and Valentino was not estopped from revoking the implied gratuitous licence in March 1993 to claim post-1993 royalties, because Hodgens suffered no relevant detriment in relation to that new royalty stream.
legal_issues: Whether section 11(3) requires intention to co-author
Whether Valentino effectively revoked the implied licence in March 1993
Whether proprietary estoppel prevented assertion of post-1993 royalty rights
Whether delay and reputational harm amounted to detriment
linked_authorities: Taylor's Fashions Ltd v Liverpool Victoria Trustees
Redwood Music Ltd v Chappell & Co Ltd

confidence.notes: Outcome, estoppel analysis, and section 11(3) ruling are clearly stated. Judge metadata in the source file appears over-inclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 costs consequences on appeal after trial offer
key_facts: Utaniko had succeeded at trial after P & O Nedlloyd rejected a Part 36 offer to accept 75% of the claim.
At trial Utaniko obtained indemnity costs and enhanced interest from July 2001 for beating that offer.
P & O Nedlloyd appealed unsuccessfully and sought to extend the Part 36 indemnity-costs regime to the appeal.
No Part 36 offer was made in the appeal proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reserved Court of Appeal judgment on costs following the substantive appeal judgment handed down on 12 February 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Respondents awarded standard-basis costs of the appeal; respondents to pay appellants' costs of the 12 February hearing, subject to set-off.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant's Part 36 offer at first instance does not automatically attract CPR 36.21 consequences on a later appeal; if a claimant wishes Part 36 protection for appeal costs it must make a separate Part 36 offer in the appeal, and absent such an offer the court will ordinarily award standard costs even where the appeal need not have been brought.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 36.21 applies to appeal proceedings by reference to a first-instance Part 36 offer
Whether the court should award indemnity costs of the appeal under CPR 44.3 by analogy with Part 36

confidence.notes: Short reserved costs judgment with a clear ratio on Part 36 and appeal costs.

enrichment.short_title: Burden of proof on deceit causation in pipeline failure
key_facts: Dalmine fraudulently certified non-compliant steel pipe used in BHP's Liverpool Bay sub-sea gas pipeline.
The pipeline failed by sulphide stress corrosion cracking only at welds adjacent to pipe with carbon equivalent above specification.
BHP sued Dalmine in deceit after its contractual claim against British Steel failed on limitation clauses.
Dalmine argued the pipeline would have failed anyway even if only compliant pipe had been installed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on burden of proof in a split trial on reliance and causation in a deceit claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; burden of proving hypothetical compliant-pipeline failure rested on Dalmine, which conceded it could not meet that burden.
enrichment.ratio: In a deceit claim where the actual pipeline failed only at non-compliant pipe and the defendant pleads that a hypothetical pipeline made solely of compliant pipe would still have failed, the defendant bears the burden of proving that counterfactual on the balance of probabilities; the claimant's general causation burden does not require it to disprove that hypothetical.
legal_issues: Allocation of burden of proof on 'but for' causation in deceit
Whether Dalmine had to prove compliant pipe would still have failed
Interaction between crack initiation and propagation caused by non-compliant CEV

linked_authorities: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital Management Committee

enrichment.short_title: Late histopathology expert refused before clinical negligence trial
key_facts: Widower John Calden sued GPs for delayed referral of his wife Amanda, who died aged 29 from aggressive breast cancer.
Defendants repeatedly resisted joint histopathology evidence and delayed expert meetings, vacating an original trial window.
After causation experts agreed tumour size based on Professor Wright's histology, defendants secretly instructed Professor Stamp.
Professor Stamp's late report was served days before a pre-trial review that fixed a May 2003 trial window.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a pre-trial review case-management order refusing late histopathology evidence and listing breach and causation for trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; trial window maintained and Professor Stamp's evidence excluded, with written questions to Professor Wright permitted.
enrichment.ratio: Where defendants caused delay, opposed histopathology evidence, and then sought at the last minute to reopen an unreserved joint experts' agreement through a newly instructed expert, the court may refuse the late evidence to preserve the trial window and overriding objective; defendants may instead put questions to the existing histopathologist and rely on their own experts' non-binding views at trial.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have fixed the trial window before ruling on late expert evidence
Whether refusal of Professor Stamp's evidence caused unfairness
Application of CPR Part 35 and Daniels v Walker to late expert evidence
Whether reopening a joint experts' agreement accorded with the overriding objective

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome and discretionary reasoning are explicit throughout the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe shotgun conviction after corrupt search officers
key_facts: Darren Christian was convicted in 1992 at the Central Criminal Court of possessing a shotgun without a firearm certificate and sentenced to three years.
His original appeal was dismissed.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case after discovering officers involved in the search and alleged discovery of the shotgun had engaged in corrupt practices.
Some officers had carried imitation weapons that could be planted to justify police actions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by reference of the Criminal Cases Review Commission under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed; defendant's costs order made for costs of the former appeal, subject to taxation.
enrichment.ratio: Where police officers involved in a search and the alleged discovery of an incriminating weapon are shown to have been engaged in a corrupt practice of carrying imitation weapons for possible planting, the safety of a conviction based on that search cannot be maintained.
legal_issues: Whether the conviction remained safe in light of corruption by officers involved in the search

confidence.notes: Outcome and basis for quashing are clear, though the judgment is brief and officer identities are deliberately withheld.

enrichment.short_title: Right of way over driveway to Coach House
key_facts: Russell trustees owned Brook House and sought to restrict Finn's vehicular access along Brook Avenue and the driveway.
Finn owned the adjacent Coach House and claimed a right of way to the south side of the Coach House, not merely to the Brook House gateposts.
Russell carried out landscaping works in 1997-2001 that blocked vehicular access along the driveway branch to the Coach House.
Finn responded with self-help works in August 2001, leading to trespass proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against first-instance declaration and injunction limiting Finn's right of way to the line between points X and Y.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; right of way held to extend along the driveway to the Coach House; reinstatement and injunctive relief ordered; Finn awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: On the true construction of the 11 October 1978 conveyance, read with the surrounding circumstance that the driveway had historically been used to access the Coach House, the granted right over Brook Avenue included the driveway branch to the Coach House and did not terminate at the Brook House gateposts.
legal_issues: Construction of the Coach House right of way in the 1978 conveyance
Relevance of pre-1978 use of the driveway as a surrounding circumstance
Whether the northern route provided alternative access
Whether a prescriptive right had been acquired
linked_authorities: St Edmundsbury Borough Council v Clark

confidence.notes: Construction issue and appeal outcome are clearly resolved on the facts found or accepted below.

enrichment.short_title: Congolese asylum and Article 8 family life appeal
key_facts: Congolese appellant Mungu claimed asylum in 1997 based on persecution linked to her husband's work for a Mobutu family bodyguard.
She lived with Mukoka, whom she claimed to have married, after he arrived separately and was granted four years' exceptional leave to remain.
The adjudicator disbelieved her account, treated her identity card as a forgery, and rejected her Article 8 claim.
The IAT upheld the adjudicator on asylum and Article 8 grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against dismissal of asylum and Article 8 appeals by the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may assess documentary and oral evidence in the round when deciding whether an asylum claim is established, without treating failure to disprove a forgery allegation as automatic proof of the document's validity; and where the adjudicator lawfully found the appellant's husband could safely return to the DRC with her, removal did not disproportionately interfere with Article 8 family life.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator reversed the burden of proof on alleged document forgery
Whether exceptional leave granted to the husband showed he could not safely return
Whether removal breached Article 8 because family life could only be enjoyed in the United Kingdom

enrichment.short_title: Recovery of overpaid severe disability premium
key_facts: Maureen Hinchy received income support including a severe disability premium while entitled to middle-rate care component of disability living allowance.
Her DLA award expired on 13 October 1998 and was not renewed, but the premium continued until 3 July 2000.
The Secretary of State sought recovery of £3,550.40 under section 71 for failure to disclose the change.
Tribunals found non-disclosure caused overpayment, though not dishonesty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against a Social Security Commissioner's decision upholding recovery of overpaid income support.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; overpayment for 13 October 1998 to 26 June 2000 held not recoverable; one-week overpayment remitted for reconsideration on misrepresentation.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 71 there is no failure to disclose a material fact already known to the Secretary of State through his own decision-makers, including the decision not to renew disability living allowance; disclosure implies revelation of something previously unknown to the decision-maker responsible for the payment.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'failure to disclose' under section 71
Whether the Secretary of State can rely on non-disclosure of facts known through DLA decisions
To whom disclosure must be made within the Department
Whether signing the order book counterfoil amounted to a section 71 misrepresentation
index_terms: Foster v Federal Commissioner of Taxation
linked_authorities: Foster v Federal Commissioner of Taxation
Bushell v Secretary of State for the Environment
Carltona Ltd v Commissioners of Works

enrichment.short_title: Costs reallocation after defective Rolls Royce hire purchase trial
key_facts: Alpha hired a defective new Rolls Royce through Lombard under a hire purchase agreement arranged by dealer H R Owen.
Alpha rescinded against Lombard and obtained restitution of £47,862; Lombard recovered £41,219 from H R Owen on a Part 20 claim but not indemnity.
H R Owen made a £15,000 Part 36 payment relating only to Alpha's direct misrepresentation claim, which failed except for £2 nominal damages.
The deputy judge ordered Lombard to bear most action costs despite H R Owen's substantive liability for the vehicle defects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal limited to costs orders following a four-day trial on liability and quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; costs orders varied so H R Owen pays Lombard's costs of the action and Part 20 proceedings, including 80% of Alpha's action costs excluding direct claims against H R Owen and the counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: Where a Part 20 defendant is in substance the unsuccessful party on the underlying defect issue, the general rule that costs follow the event should not be displaced merely because it made a Part 36 payment on a separate direct claim that failed, nor because the Part 20 claimant persisted in defending the main action while liability was denied.
legal_issues: Whether a first-instance Part 36 payment on the direct claim justified Alpha paying H R Owen's post-payment costs
Whether Lombard rather than H R Owen should bear the costs of Alpha's successful claim against Lombard
Discretion under CPR 44.3 where multiple claims and a Part 20 claim were tried together

confidence.notes: Substantive findings were not appealed; the judgment focuses clearly on correcting the costs discretion.
